ST.004Team/Decisions/Co-founders

He started the company with his best friend from college. Then he asked him to leave

Two founders, equal titles, equal shares. By the time they had 30 employees, nobody could make the final call.

Interview
Takuma NakamuraLANTERN Inc.　CEO
Interview & text
SECOND TAKE
Date
Sep 22, 2026
Read
7 min

In this story

  1. 01Fifty-fifty
  2. 02No decisions
  3. 03Six months
  4. 04Once a year

In briefThe decision in three lines

  1. With equal shares and equal authority, nobody had the final say.
  2. After six months of talks, he asked his co-founder to step down.
  3. They still go out for a drink together once a year.

Partway through the interview, Takuma Nakamura went quiet. It was the moment he said his co-founder’s name.

We were on the fourth floor of an old office building in Kanda, Tokyo. He held his teacup in both hands and took a while to find the words.

The two met in a university seminar and started the company at 27. They split the capital and the titles exactly down the middle. At the time, he genuinely believed that was the fairest way.

Scene 01Fifty-fifty seemed fair

Equal shares and equal authority is unusual.

NakamuraPeople told us not to. But I didn’t want to decide who was on top. Without him, I wouldn’t have started the company at all.

And for a while it worked.

NakamuraThe first five years were genuinely fun. I sold, he built. We’d argue, and by the evening we’d be eating ramen together.

Things changed once they passed 30 employees. Hiring standards, when to raise prices, whether to put people on a new product. When the two disagreed, the meeting simply stopped.

Scene 02Weekly meetings that decided nothing

What happened when you disagreed?

NakamuraWe postponed. Pushed it to the next week, disagreed again, pushed it again. The team didn’t know whose face to read anymore.

NakamuraOne day a manager told me, “Until the two of you agree, we can’t do anything.” He didn’t say it as a complaint. That made it worse.

That night Nakamura sent his co-founder a message that said only, “We need to talk.” The reply: “Me too.”

Scene 03Six months before he could say it

Did you raise the idea of him leaving right away?

NakamuraNo. At first I thought we could split roles — me on the business, him leading engineering. But even then, the final call still sat with both of us.

NakamuraFor about six months we met once a week outside the office. In the end, he was the one who said, “This won’t end unless one of us steps down.” Maybe I was waiting for him to say it. That still bothers me a little.

His co-founder left the board while keeping part of his stake. Six months later he became CTO at another company.

Scene 04A drink, once a year

How are things between you now?

NakamuraOnce a year, on the day we founded the company, we go out for a drink. We barely talk about work. Mostly I listen to him complain about his company.

If you started again, would you set it up the same way?

NakamuraNo. Starting a company with a friend is fine. But decide up front who makes the final call. If that breaks the friendship, you probably shouldn’t have started together.
